new.headline: Skip the extra 16-miler: your fitness is built, and heavy legs this week are what a taper feels like. Keep race week short with one small dose of race pace, then average 8:33 to 8:34 per mile on Sunday.

answers.question: Is it crazy to do one more 16-miler on Wednesday so I feel ready?
answers.answer:
Yes, it would hurt more than it helps, so leave it out. A long run four days before a marathon takes about a week to recover from, and you would start the race still carrying it.

Your 20-milers on Sun Sep 13 and Sun Oct 4 already built the endurance, and one more run cannot add to it in time. For the confidence you are after, the 2 miles at race pace on Wednesday do the job. They show the pace is there and leave your legs fresh.

new.analysis:
Last week followed the plan on every day, so the training behind you is clean. Each run matched its planned distance, the rest days stayed rest days, and the week came to 34 mi, down from 46 mi. That is a normal first taper step.

Your numbers show fitness holding, not fading. Easy runs stayed at 9:52 per mile and 139 bpm, the same as for the last four weeks. The race-pace block on Wed Oct 7 averaged 8:36 per mile with no fade, and pain was 0/10 all week.

The flat, heavy feeling fits a taper. Legs often feel dull in the last week while the body sheds fatigue, and freshness usually arrives in the final two or three days. Fitness fades over weeks, not over one lighter week.

Race week is built to keep your legs sharp without adding fatigue. It holds about 17 mi of running before the race, one short touch of race pace and a few strides. You have nothing left to gain from training, so the job now is to arrive fresh.

The pace target needs care, because 8:35 per mile finishes a few seconds over 3:45. The table shows what each average pace gives you over 26.2 mi.

| Average pace per mile | Finish time |
| --- | --- |
| 8:30 | 3:42:52 |
| 8:32 | 3:43:44 |
| 8:34 | 3:44:36 |
| 8:35 | 3:45:03 |
| 8:36 | 3:45:29 |

Your race-pace miles on Wed Oct 7 at 8:36 would just miss. Starting at 8:40 to 8:45 for 3 miles and then holding 8:33 still finishes around 3:44:30, which leaves about 30 seconds in hand. That patient start also protects the last 6 miles, which is where most marathons are won or lost.
